title: Custom kernel fallback policy and KV affinity draft
content:
Purpose

This is an exploratory working doc to capture experiments and design notes for a combined approach to: (1) using TensorRT engines and Triton backends alongside our custom CUDA kernels, and (2) placing and routing KV cache state to improve end-to-end latency and tail behavior. The goal is to propose a pragmatic fallback policy and KV affinity heuristics that reduce 99th percentile latency regressions when engines are cold or when kernel compatibility issues occur.

Background / motivation

We have three classes of execution targets in the fleet today: Triton-managed model instances (non-TRT), TensorRT serialized engines (TRT runtime), and our custom CUDA operator pipeline (custom-kernel). Each has distinct perf/latency/cold-start profiles:
- Triton (non-TRT): predictable scheduling, supports multi-instance, slower per-token latency on some FP16/INT8 paths but fast startup.
- TRT engines: high steady-state throughput/low per-token latency, long compile+serialization time for kernels and optimization (especially for long context lengths) and fragile to model-ops changes.
- Custom kernels: flexible (supports new ops, dynamic shapes), mid-range latency, fastest iteration for infra changes.

Operational problem: when requests are routed to the fastest steady-state target (TRT) but the engine is cold or unavailable, naive fallbacks to Triton or custom-kernel can cause large latency spikes because cached KV state is not local, or because the fallback target has different KV layout expectations.

Design goals (non-exhaustive)
- Keep 95th/99th latency within SLOs under mixed traffic (chat + completion).
- Avoid costly synchronous KV migrations during per-request fallback. Prefer cache-affinity preserving fallbacks.
- Minimize model-quality divergence: fallback should preserve deterministic decoding behavior where possible.
- Make policy inexpensive to evaluate per-request (no expensive DP or search).

Experiment setup (summary)

Hardware and baseline software
- GPUs: A100 40GB (primary testbed), RTX6000 variant for dev.
- Triton: 24.02 release with dynamic batching disabled for isolation.
- TensorRT: 9.4.2 for engine builds.
- Runtime: branch "engine-fallback-proto" (see PR in linked_artifacts).

Workloads
- Chat workload (multi-turn, average prompt 150 tokens, KV reuse high).
- Completion workload (single-turn, long generation ~1024 tokens).
- Mix: 70% chat / 30% completion to stress KV reuse paths.

Key knobs exercised
- KV placement: shared-NVM cache (slow), local-GPU-KV (fast), memory-backed per-engine KV copy (fast but high memory).
- Fallback policy: hard-fallback (instant reroute), soft-fallback (attempt warm-up + buffered fallback), staged-fallback (try replica TRT engine, then custom-kernel).
- Affinity windows: per-user-per-session sticky lifetime (e.g., 5 min / 30 min), per-request ephemeral.
- Pre-warm heuristics: probabilistic prefetch for top-k actors after idle timeout.

New heuristics we tried
- KV-affinity-first: prefer fallback target that already has matching KV keys (prefix match on session id). If none, prefer targets that have recently seen same model version within the region.
- Engine-warm-probing: on an engine miss, asynchronously schedule a low-priority probe to build the TRT engine while immediately serving from custom-kernel; subsequent requests can route once TRT is ready.
- Soft-decode-policy: when falling back to custom-kernel, use identical decoding hyperparams; when switching to Triton non-TRT, enforce deterministic sampling mode to avoid quality divergence.

Measured results (high level)

Note: microbench numbers below are median across 5 runs; tail numbers are from a 60-minute synthetic run with arrival bursts.

- Cold TRT engine compile (A100): 22–34s median compile time for medium-sized encoder-decoder (context 2048); worst-case observed 58s.
- Async probe (non-blocking): probe build CPU/GPU slot cost ~0.7x a standard inference batch for the build phase; with low-priority we observed <2% interference on colocated serving tasks.
- KV-affinity-first fallback: reduced 99th percentile latency by 18–32% compared to hard fallback (numbers vary by workload). Improvements driven by avoiding cross-target KV fetches that added 20–120ms per request.
- Staged-fallback (TRT-replica then custom): best tradeoff for chat-heavy traffic; kept token latency within 1.05x steady-state median while avoiding 99th percentile spikes.
- Memory cost: maintaining per-engine KV copies increased GPU memory by 6–9% for chat-heavy sessions across experiments; acceptable on large instances but not viable on low-memory nodes.

Tradeoffs and observations

1) Warm vs cold engines
- TRT engines are excellent once ready; however the cold-compile tax is large and unpredictable for longer context models. That makes synchronous fallback unacceptable for user-facing low-latency paths.

2) KV placement matters more than kernel choice for tail latency
- Experiments where fallback was constrained to targets that already had KV affinity consistently outperformed faster kernel choices without affinity. Cross-node KV fetches were often the dominant tail source.

3) Soft vs hard fallback
- Soft strategies (serve from an available target while background-warming the preferred target) reduce tail latency and improve median experience, at cost of increased engineering complexity (state tracking, background job scheduling).

4) Memory vs latency tradeoff
- Keeping duplicate KV copies reduces migration cost but increases working set size. For high-value sessions (paying customers / low-latency routes) this can be a configurable per-route policy.

Recommended fallback policy (initial proposal)

Rule evaluation is evaluated in this order and is intended to be cheaply computable at routing time:
1) If target (TRT engine) is warm and has KV affinity for session -> route to TRT.
2) Else if a TRT replica in region is warm and affinity exists -> route to TRT replica.
3) Else if an engine probe is already in-progress for this session/model -> soft fallback: serve from custom-kernel and mark request with probe-timestamp (for metrics).
4) Else if session has strong KV affinity on custom-kernel instance -> route to custom-kernel.
5) Else stream to Triton non-TRT if decoding determinism must be preserved; otherwise route to custom-kernel.
6) Simultaneously schedule an async engine-warm probe if TRT is the preferred steady-state route.

Implementation notes and data structures

- Session affinity table (in control plane cache): maps session-id -> last-seen-node, model-version, KV-checksum. Keep TTL-based expiry (default 30m). Cheap checksum is 64-bit of the KV prefix.
- Probe registry: lightweight entry per session+model with state {in-progress, started_at, target_engine_id}. Keep registry capped by LRU and scaled by region.
- Route decision must be atomic-ish: store-and-forward operations should tolerate eventual consistency, so route timestamps must be included on requests for observability.

Corner cases and risks

- Model rollout churn: TRT serialized engines may fail to load after minor model op changes. Must attach robust failure classification and auto-rollback of probe attempts.
- Stale affinity: session-id reuse across devices can cause affinity mismatches; TTL tuning required.
- Cost of probes: if probes are overused they will increase GPU churn and reduce overall throughput. We must limit probe concurrency per node.
- Consistency of KV encoding across runtimes: ensure our KV serialization format is stable and versioned; include a version header in cached KV blobs.

Operational metrics to monitor (recommended)

- Per-route 50/95/99 latency broken out by target type (TRT, Triton, custom).
- Probe success rate and average build time.
- KV-affinity hit rate and mean extra fetch time when affinity-miss.
- Memory overhead from duplicated KV copies per node.
- Number of concurrent probes per node and per-region.

Short-term next steps (actionable)

1) Implement session affinity table + probe registry prototype (PR created, see linked_artifacts).
2) Wire soft-fallback telemetry flags so product experiments can gate the policy by route.
3) Add aggressive TTL tuning experiment per-customer (5m, 30m, 2h) to find sweet spot for chat workload.
4) Run a controlled canary on 5% fleet with staged-fallback enabled for chat-only routes and collect 72h telemetry.

Open questions (for engineering & product)

- Should KV duplication be priced as a premium option (cost center) or be an infra-level optimization for SLO-critical customers?
- How aggressive should probe concurrency caps be per GPU? (Experiment with 2/4/8)
- Is there a simpler canonical checksum for KV match that balances false positives/negatives?

Notes to reviewers

This doc is intentionally informal. Please comment inline with experimental concerns, and add known failure modes from your subsystem (e.g., Triton dynamic-shape signals, scheduler preemption policies). If you have recent cluster traces showing affinity-miss tail events, paste timestamps or links in the PR for cross-validation.

Appendix: quick command snippets used

- Build TRT engine (dev harness): ./tools/build_trt_engine.sh --model mymodel.onnx --max_seq_len 2048 --workspace 40GB
- Start probe job (local): curl -XPOST https://runtime-internal/api/probe -d '{"session":"abc123","model":"mymodel","priority":"low"}'
